mainTopic: Burning נותר on יום טוב, which soft parts of the קרבן פסח count as meat, and lashes for breaking a bone of the פסח
overview: This amud begins by finishing the discussion of why leftover meat of the קרבן פסח (נותר) is not burned on יום טוב. רב אשי explains that יום טוב has both an עשה and a לא תעשה, and the single עשה of burning cannot override both. Then a new משנה teaches which soft parts of the קרבן פסח count as edible meat. רבה finds a contradiction inside the משנה and solves it by splitting it between two תנאים. רבא instead reads it as one rule: what boiling makes edible in a grown ox, roasting makes edible in a young kid. A ברייתא supports רבא. רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש then argue about sinews that will later harden, which turns on whether we judge by the present or by the end. רבי יוחנן is shown to have retracted and agreed with ריש לקיש. A second משנה rules that breaking a bone of a pure פסח earns forty lashes, while leaving over meat or breaking a bone of an impure פסח does not. The גמרא gives the sources for both exemptions and brings a dispute between the תנא קמא and רבי about how to derive the bone rule. רבי ירמיה starts to explain the practical difference, a פסח brought in טומאה, and his explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A Delayed ברית מילה Does Not Override יום טוב
steps.stepSummary: The closing words of a source teaching that a ברית מילה done after the eighth day does not push aside שבת or יום טוב, even though one might have argued that it should through a קל וחומר.
steps.simpleTranslation: ...and not a circumcision that is not at its proper time, which would otherwise have been derived through a קל וחומר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a source it was quoting. The source says the Torah's word 'on the day' excludes a late ברית מילה from overriding שבת and יום טוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברית מילה done on the eighth day overrides שבת. One might have reasoned with a קל וחומר that even a late מילה should override, since מילה is strong enough to override other laws such as cutting off a צרעת mark. The verse is needed to block that reasoning. A late מילה does not override, because it is not tied to one specific day.

keyTerms.meaning: A circumcision done after its proper time, the eighth day
An argument from a lighter case to a stricter case

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not the start of a new topic. It is the end of a source the גמרא was already quoting in its discussion of burning נותר on יום טוב.

phrases.english: and not a circumcision that is not at its proper time,
phrases.notes: A ברית done after the eighth day.

phrases.english: which would come through an a fortiori argument.
phrases.notes: Without the verse, a קל וחומר would have suggested it overrides.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes a source quoted in the previous part of the sugya (on the previous amud).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ברית מילה performed after its proper time does not override שבת or יום טוב.

steps.title: רב אשי's Reason: יום טוב Has Both a Positive and a Negative Command
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that נותר is not burned on יום טוב because the positive command to burn it cannot override both the positive command and the prohibition of יום טוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The word 'שבתון' (a day of rest) said about יום טוב is a positive command, and a positive command does not push aside a combination of a prohibition plus a positive command.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers a different reason why leftover קרבן פסח meat is not burned on יום טוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally an עשה can override a לא תעשה (עשה דוחה לא תעשה). On יום טוב, though, there is also a positive command to rest, learned from the word 'שבתון'. Two commands stand against the burning, so the single עשה of burning נותר is not strong enough to override them.

keyTerms.meaning: A day of solemn rest; here it creates a positive command to rest

steps.whatToRemember: An עשה can override a plain לא תעשה, but it cannot override a לא תעשה combined with an עשה. That is why נותר is not burned on יום טוב according to רב אשי.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule אין עשה דוחה לא תעשה ועשה is a general principle used throughout ש״ס.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
'Solemn rest' of a Festival is a positive command,
and a positive command does not override
phrases.notes: Here this refers to the command to burn נותר.

phrases.english: a prohibition together with a positive command.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an alternative explanation to the previous derivations for why נותר is not burned on יום טוב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Burning נותר does not override יום טוב, because יום טוב has both an עשה (שבתון) and a לא תעשה, and an עשה cannot override both.

steps.title: New משנה: What Counts as Edible in the קרבן פסח
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that whatever is edible in a grown ox counts as edible in a young kid, and that the soft rib-tips and cartilage may be eaten.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Anything that is eaten in a fully grown ox may be eaten in a young tender kid, and so may the ends of the ribs and the cartilage.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It defines which parts of the קרבן פסח count as real 'meat' that can be eaten as part of the מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The standard for 'edible' is set by a grown ox. In a grown ox, the bones and hard parts have fully hardened. Any part that is food there counts as food in a young kid too. The משנה then adds that the soft rib-tips and cartilage may be eaten.

keyTerms.meaning: A fully grown ox, whose bones have hardened
The soft ends of the ribs

phrases.english: MISHNA: Anything that is eaten in an adult ox —
may be eaten in a young kid,
phrases.notes: It counts as meat of the קרבן פסח.

phrases.english: and the ends of the ribs and the cartilage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic unrelated to the previous discussion about burning נותר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The edibility of parts of the קרבן פסח is measured by a grown ox; rib-tips and cartilage may be eaten.

steps.title: רבה Finds a Contradiction Between the Two Clauses of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: רבה infers from the first clause that only parts edible in a grown ox count. That seems to clash with the second clause, which permits rib-tips and cartilage, parts that are not edible in a grown ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רבה raised a contradiction. We learned: 'Anything that is eaten in a grown ox may be eaten in a young kid.' This implies that what is not eaten in a grown ox is not eaten. But say the latter clause: 'the ends of the ribs and the cartilage.' These are not eaten in a grown ox!
steps.whatsHappening: רבה points out that the first part of the משנה seems to contradict the second part. The גמרא will need to resolve this in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From the רישא, רבה draws an inference (דיוק): if only what is edible in a grown ox counts, then anything inedible in a grown ox should not count. Yet the סיפא allows rib-tips and cartilage. In a grown ox these have already hardened like bone and are not eaten. So the סיפא appears to break the rule set by the רישא.
steps.confusionAlert: The first clause never actually says 'what is not eaten in an ox is forbidden.' That is רבה's inference from its wording, and it is the inference that creates the clash.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rabba raised a contradiction: We learned:
Anything that is eaten in an adult ox —
may be eaten in a young kid,
but what is not eaten (in an ox) — not.
phrases.notes: This is רבה's inference from the רישא.

phrases.english: Say the latter clause:
the ends of the ribs and the cartilage.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא הָנֵי לָא מִתְאַכְלִי בְּשׁוֹר הַגָּדוֹל!
phrases.english: But these are not eaten in an adult ox!
phrases.notes: In a grown ox they have hardened like bone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the internal consistency of the משנה just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two clauses of the משנה (רישא versus סיפא).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רישא implies that parts inedible in a grown ox do not count, but the סיפא permits rib-tips and cartilage, which are inedible in a grown ox.

steps.title: רבה resolves the contradiction by splitting the משנה into two opinions
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers his own question. The two clauses of the משנה come from two different תנאים. The first view forbids rib-tips and cartilage, and a second view (יש אומרים) permits them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is a dispute between תנאים, and this is what the משנה is teaching: anything eaten in a grown ox may be eaten in a young kid, and anything not eaten in a grown ox may not. And some say: even the rib-tips and the cartilage may be eaten.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה fixes the contradiction he raised. He says the two halves of the משנה are not one opinion but two different opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first clause sets a strict test: only what is edible in a grown ox counts. The second clause, which allows rib-tips and cartilage, belongs to a different opinion that disagrees. Because the clauses come from different speakers, they no longer contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (rejects the assumption that both clauses are one opinion)
It is a dispute between תנאים
And this is what it is teaching (a re-reading of the משנה)

steps.confusionAlert: Our printed משנה does not actually say 'יש אומרים'. רבה is re-reading the משנה as if the second clause were a separate opinion.

phrases.english: Rather, it is a dispute between Tannaim,
and this is what it is teaching:
Anything eaten in a grown ox —
may be eaten in a young kid,
and what is not eaten [in a grown ox] — not.
phrases.notes: First opinion: a strict test based on the grown ox.

phrases.english: And some say:
even the rib-tips and the cartilage.
phrases.notes: Second opinion. These parts can become edible in an ox through long cooking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction רבה raised in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the source between two different authorities (תנאי היא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both clauses of the משנה are one opinion, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first clause is one תנא's strict view, and the second clause is a different תנא who permits rib-tips and cartilage.

steps.title: רבא reads the second clause as a list explaining the first
steps.stepSummary: רבא keeps the משנה as one opinion. The rule means that what a grown ox makes edible by boiling, a young kid makes edible by roasting. The rib-tips and cartilage are examples of this rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: the משנה teaches in the style of 'what are they', and this is what it is teaching: anything eaten in a grown ox through boiling may be eaten in a young kid through roasting. And what are these parts? The rib-tips and the cartilage.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא offers a different answer to the same contradiction. In his reading the משנה is one opinion, and the second clause simply lists examples of the first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key change is reading the first clause as 'boiled in an ox' versus 'roasted in a kid.' A קרבן פסח may only be eaten roasted. Rib-tips and cartilage of a grown ox become soft only after boiling, while in a young kid they are already soft enough to eat roasted. So the second clause does not contradict the first. It gives examples of it.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches 'what are they' (a general rule followed by its examples)
Roasting (the only permitted way to eat the קרבן פסח)

steps.whyThisMatters: Bringing in בשלקא and בצלי ties the משנה directly to the rule that the קרבן פסח must be eaten roasted.

phrases.english: Rava said: It teaches 'what are they,'
phrases.notes: The second clause explains the first rather than adding a new ruling.

phrases.english: and this is what it is teaching:
Anything eaten in a grown ox through boiling —
may be eaten in a young kid through roasting.
And what are they?
The rib-tips and the cartilage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, competing answer to step 4's contradiction, different from רבה's in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the structure of the משנה (general rule followed by its examples)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first clause means 'edible in an ox' in any way, so rib-tips and cartilage seem to be excluded.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first clause means 'edible in an ox by boiling,' and this exactly includes rib-tips and cartilage, which the young kid has soft enough to eat roasted.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבא and adds that soft sinews count as meat
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא uses the exact wording of רבא's reading, which supports him. It also adds a new point: soft sinews are treated as meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא in line with רבא: anything eaten in a grown ox through boiling may be eaten in a young kid through roasting. And what are they? The rib-tips and the cartilage. And soft sinews are judged as meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says word-for-word what רבא said. This proves his reading is correct.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא has the very phrases רבא proposed: בשלקא, בצלי, and ומה הן. It also adds something new: soft sinews count as meat. That addition sets up the next dispute about sinews that are soft now but will harden later.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught (in a ברייתא) in line with his view

steps.whatToRemember: Final reading of the משנה, following רבא and the ברייתא: what is edible in a grown ox by boiling is edible in a young kid by roasting. This includes rib-tips, cartilage, and soft sinews.

phrases.english: It was taught in accordance with Rava:
Anything eaten in a grown ox through boiling —
may be eaten in a young kid through roasting,
and what are they? The rib-tips and the cartilage,
and soft sinews are judged as meat.
phrases.notes: A new detail, not found in the משנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא's answer from step 6.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's reading of the משנה (boiled in an ox equals roasted in a kid, with ומה הן listing the examples)
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that has the identical wording

steps.title: Dispute over sinews that are soft now but will harden later
steps.stepSummary: Using an איתמר, the גמרא reports a dispute. רבי יוחנן says one may join a group for a קרבן פסח based on sinews that will later harden. ריש לקיש says one may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: about sinews that will eventually harden, רבי יוחנן said one may register for them in the קרבן פסח, and ריש לקיש said one may not register for them in the קרבן פסח.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new related question. Do sinews that are soft now but will harden later count as meat, so that a person can sign up for the קרבן פסח just for that portion?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said soft sinews count as meat. Now the case is harder: the sinews are soft today but will become hard and inedible. רבי יוחנן counts them as meat, and ריש לקיש does not.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces a dispute between אמוראים)
One may register (sign up as a member) for them

steps.confusionAlert: נמנין means signing up as one of the people who share the קרבן פסח. A person must register for a portion of edible meat, so the question is whether these sinews count as that portion.

phrases.english: It was stated: sinews that will eventually harden,

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: נִמְנִין עֲלֵיהֶן בַּפֶּסַח,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said: one may register for them in the Pesach offering,

phrases.aramaic: רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר: אֵין נִמְנִין עֲלֵיהֶן בַּפֶּסַח.
phrases.english: Reish Lakish said: one may not register for them in the Pesach offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the ברייתא's ruling about soft sinews and moves to a harder case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן: one may register for sinews that will later harden. ריש לקיש: one may not.

steps.title: The reasoning: present state versus final state
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the dispute. רבי יוחנן judges the sinews by how they are now, which is soft. ריש לקיש judges them by how they will end up, which is hard.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said one may register for them because we follow the present state. ריש לקיש said one may not register for them because we follow the final state.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reason behind each side of the dispute. It is a question of which moment matters: now, or later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Right now the sinews are soft and edible, so רבי יוחנן counts them as meat. ריש לקיש looks at what they will become, which is hard and not food, so for him they are not meat even now. The whole dispute comes down to one principle: בתר השתא versus בתר בסוף.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן judges by the present (השתא), and ריש לקיש judges by the end result (סוף). This is a general way of thinking that comes up in many places in ש״ס.
steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of judging something by its present state versus its future state is a recurring theme across ש״ס.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said one may register for them —
we follow the present [state].

phrases.aramaic: רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר אֵין נִמְנִין עֲלֵיהֶן —
phrases.english: Reish Lakish said one may not register for them —
we follow the end [state].

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר נִמְנִין עֲלֵיהֶן בָּתַר הַשְׁתָּא אָזְלִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind each side of the dispute in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dispute depends on whether we judge by the present (השתא) or by the final state (סוף).

steps.title: ריש לקיש challenges רבי יוחנן from the ברייתא's list
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש quotes the ברייתא. It lists only rib-tips and cartilage, which implies that sinews that will harden are not counted as meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש challenged ר' יוחנן: 'Whatever is eaten in a grown ox is eaten in a young kid. And what are these? The rib-tips and the cartilage.' These parts, yes, but sinews that will later harden, no!
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש quotes the 'ומה הן' teaching from step 7, the ברייתא that supported רבא. He uses it to attack ר' יוחנן's ruling that one may join a פסח group based on sinews that will later harden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The quoted source names only two examples, rib-tips and cartilage. ריש לקיש reads that list as complete, so sinews that will harden are left out. If they were left out, they do not count as meat, which goes against ר' יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection to him, usually from a תנאי source
Rib-tips, the soft ends of the ribs

phrases.english: Reish Lakish raised an objection to Rabbi Yochanan:
Anything eaten in a grown ox
may be eaten in a young kid,
and what are these? The rib-tips and the cartilage.
phrases.notes: This is the same ברייתא that supported רבא in step 7.

phrases.english: These, yes,
but sinews that will eventually harden, no!
phrases.notes: This is ריש לקיש's inference from what the list leaves out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It attacks ר' יוחנן's side of the dispute presented in steps 8 and 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: ר' יוחנן's ruling that one may join a פסח group based on sinews that will harden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's list is read as complete. Sinews are not on it, so they must not count as meat.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the list is only examples, and sinews share the same reason
steps.stepSummary: ר' יוחנן answers that the ברייתא gave sample cases. Sinews fit the same rule, because they too become edible when a grown ox is boiled.
steps.simpleTranslation: ר' יוחנן said to him: It taught these, and the same law applies to those. What is the reason for these? Because they are eaten in a grown ox through boiling. Those, the sinews, are also eaten in a grown ox through boiling.
steps.whatsHappening: ר' יוחנן defends himself. The ברייתא's list was never meant to be complete.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source gives a principle: what boiling makes edible in an ox, roasting makes edible in a kid. Sinews that will harden meet that principle exactly as rib-tips do, since they too are edible in a grown ox through boiling. So leaving them off the list proves nothing.

phrases.english: He said to him: It taught these
and the same is true for those.
What is the reason for these?
Because they are eaten in a grown ox through boiling,

phrases.aramaic: הָנָךְ נָמֵי מִתְאַכְלִי בְּשׁוֹר הַגָּדוֹל בְּשִׁלְקָא.
phrases.english: those too are eaten in a grown ox through boiling.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: תְּנָא הָנֵי וְהוּא הַדִּין לְהָנָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It answers ריש לקיש's challenge in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The list is read as examples, not as a complete list.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'ומה הן' list names every part that counts, so sinews that will harden are excluded.
steps.terutzMaskana: The list gives sample cases of a rule ('edible in a grown ox through boiling'), and sinews that will harden fall under the same rule.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה points out a contradiction in רבי יוחנן's views
steps.stepSummary: ר' ירמיה notes a problem. On sinews, ר' יוחנן judges by the present. On the scalp-skin of a young calf, he ruled it cannot become טמא as food, which judges by the end.
steps.simpleTranslation: ר' ירמיה said to ר' אבין: When you go before ר' אבהו, ask him this contradiction. Did ר' יוחנן really say that people may register for a פסח based on sinews that will harden? That would mean we follow the present state. But ריש לקיש asked ר' יוחנן: Can the scalp-skin of a young calf become טמא as food? And he answered: It does not become טמא. That means we follow the final state!
steps.whatsHappening: ר' ירמיה sends a question through ר' אבין to ר' אבהו. ר' יוחנן seems to contradict himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The scalp-skin of a young calf is soft and edible now, but it will later become tough hide. Ruling that it does not receive טומאת אוכלין means ר' יוחנן treated it by its future state as hide. That clashes with his sinew ruling, which follows the present state.

keyTerms.meaning: The scalp-skin of a young calf
That it becomes טמא, here as food

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה לְרַבִּי אָבִין:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said to Rabbi Avin:
When you go before Rabbi Abbahu,
raise this contradiction to him:
Did Rabbi Yochanan really say
that sinews that will eventually harden,
people may register for them in the Pesach offering,
which shows that we go by the present state?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: But Reish Lakish asked Rabbi Yochanan:
The hide of the head of a young calf,
can it become ritually impure, as food?
And he said to him: It does not become impure.
This shows that we go by the final state!

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אָזְלַתְּ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ, רְמִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After ר' יוחנן's view is defended from the ברייתא, it is now challenged from his own ruling in another case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The consistency of ר' יוחנן's position
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In one case ר' יוחנן follows the present state and in another he follows the final state. These two rulings cannot both stand on one principle.
steps.confusionAlert: Both cases share one question: do we judge a soft part by what it is now or by what it will become? On sinews ר' יוחנן says 'now.' On the calf's scalp-skin he seems to say 'later.'

steps.title: רבי אבהו: רבי יוחנן retracted and agreed with ריש לקיש
steps.stepSummary: ר' אבהו says the questioner did not think it through. ר' יוחנן later retracted his view and agreed with ריש לקיש, saying that the source he had relied on was only a lone opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: ר' אבהו said to him: Whoever asked you this did not care about his flour. ר' יוחנן retracted and agreed with ריש לקיש, and said to him: 'Do not trouble me, for I teach that source as a single opinion.'
steps.whatsHappening: ר' אבהו resolves the contradiction. ר' יוחנן's sinew ruling was his earlier view, and he later changed his mind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'He did not care about his flour' means the questioner did not sift his question carefully. In the end ר' יוחנן agreed with ריש לקיש that we follow the final state. He set aside the source that had seemed to support following the present state, calling it the view of one individual. So the scalp-skin ruling is his final view, and the sinew ruling was dropped.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not care about his flour, meaning he did not think carefully
Do not trouble or provoke me
As the view of a single individual

steps.whatToRemember: ר' יוחנן's final view matches ריש לקיש: we judge an animal part by its final state. So sinews that will harden do not count for joining a פסח group.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that an אמורא's earlier ruling can be overturned by his later retraction. It explains how the גמרא settles an apparent contradiction without forcing a fine distinction between the two cases.

phrases.english: He said to him: The one who raised this contradiction to you
was not concerned for his flour.
phrases.notes: An idiom for not carefully sifting one's words.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan retracted
in favor of Reish Lakish,
and said to him: Do not trouble me,
for I teach it in the singular.
phrases.notes: The source he had relied on is only one Sage's opinion and is not binding.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּרְמָא לָךְ הָא לָא חַשׁ לְקִמְחֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It answers the contradiction raised in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Retraction: the earlier ruling was abandoned.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ר' יוחנן holds both rulings at once, so he contradicts himself.
steps.terutzMaskana: ר' יוחנן retracted and agreed with ריש לקיש to follow the final state. The sinew ruling was from before his retraction.

steps.title: New משנה: lashes for breaking a bone of a pure פסח
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה begins. Breaking a bone of a pure פסח earns forty lashes, but leaving over meat from a pure פסח, or breaking a bone of an impure פסח, does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who breaks a bone of a pure פסח receives forty lashes. But one who leaves over meat from a pure פסח, or one who breaks a bone of an impure פסח, does not receive the forty lashes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new משנה. It deals with which violations of the פסח laws earn מלקות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Breaking a bone of a pure פסח violates a לאו, so מלקות apply. Leaving over meat (נותר) is different, and so is breaking a bone of a פסח that became impure and is now disqualified. Neither earns lashes, and the גמרא will explain why.

keyTerms.meaning: One who leaves over meat past its time (נותר)
Ritually impure, here a פסח that became impure and is therefore פסול

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who breaks the bone of a ritually pure Pesach offering
receives forty lashes.
But one who leaves over meat of a pure one
and one who breaks a bone of an impure one
does not receive the forty lashes.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַשּׁוֹבֵר אֶת הָעֶצֶם בַּפֶּסַח הַטָּהוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It starts a new topic and is not connected to the sinew discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Breaking a bone of a pure פסח earns forty lashes. Leaving over meat from a pure פסח, or breaking a bone of an impure פסח, does not.

steps.title: Why leaving over a pure פסח gets no lashes: רבי יהודה's reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the משנה's first ruling and supports it with a ברייתא. Per רבי יהודה, the Torah attached a positive command (burn the leftovers) to the prohibition, so there are no lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: It makes sense that one who leaves over a pure פסח is not lashed, as a ברייתא teaches: 'Do not leave any of it until morning, and what remains of it until morning you shall burn.' The verse places a positive command after the prohibition to teach that one is not lashed. These are the words of רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts on the משנה and shows that the first ruling (no lashes for leaving over a pure פסח) has a clear source. The word בשלמא ('granted') signals that a harder question about the other ruling is coming next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah first says 'do not leave over' and then says 'burn what is left.' A prohibition that can be fixed by doing a positive command is a לאו הניתק לעשה, and there are no lashes for it. That is רבי יהודה's reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted / it makes sense (sets up a question on something else)
One who leaves over meat past the allowed time
A positive command placed after a prohibition
A prohibition that can be fixed by a positive command, which carries no lashes

steps.confusionAlert: בשלמא does not mean the גמרא is finished. It means 'this part is fine,' and it prepares a question on the next part of the משנה.

phrases.english: GEMARA
Granted, one who leaves over from a pure [Pesach] is not lashed,
as it was taught in a baraita:
"You shall not leave any of it until morning,
and what remains of it until morning, etc." [you shall burn]
The verse comes to place a positive command
after a prohibition,
to say that one is not lashed.
These are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא on the משנה from step 14 by sourcing its first ruling.
steps.raayaObject: The משנה's ruling that leaving over a pure פסח carries no lashes
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא on שמות יב:י, as explained by רבי יהודה (לאו הניתק לעשה)

steps.title: רבי יעקב's different reason: no action was done
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב agrees there are no lashes but gives another reason. Leaving over involves no action, and there are no lashes for a לאו שאין בו מעשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב says: That is not the reason. Rather, it is a prohibition that involves no action, and one is not lashed for such a prohibition.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues. רבי יעקב reaches the same result (no lashes) for a different reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving meat over is a failure to eat it, not something a person actively does. רבי יעקב holds that lashes require an action, so this prohibition carries none. Both תנאים agree on the ruling and disagree only on the reason.

keyTerms.meaning: This is not for that reason
A prohibition broken without any action
One is not lashed for it

phrases.english: Rabbi Yaakov says:
This is not for that reason;
rather, it is because it is
a prohibition that involves no action,
and one is not lashed for it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר לֹא מִן הַשֵּׁם הוּא זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternative reason, within the same ברייתא, for the same ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are no lashes for leaving over, because it is a לאו שאין בו מעשה.

steps.title: What is the source for no lashes when breaking a bone of an impure פסח?
steps.stepSummary: Leaving over is explained, but the גמרא now asks for the source that breaking a bone of an impure פסח carries no lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: But one who breaks a bone of an impure פסח, how do we know he is not lashed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks the question that בשלמא was preparing. Breaking a bone is a real action, so neither earlier reason works here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Breaking a bone is an action, and the Torah attaches no positive command to fix it. So a new source is needed for why breaking a bone of an impure פסח carries no lashes.

keyTerms.meaning: One who breaks a bone of an impure פסח
From where do we know this?

phrases.english: But one who breaks [a bone] of an impure [Pesach],
from where do we know [he is not lashed]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the בשלמא contrast by turning to the משנה's second exemption.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source exempting one who breaks a bone of an impure פסח

steps.title: The word 'in it' limits the prohibition to a valid פסח
steps.stepSummary: The verse says 'do not break a bone in it,' and 'in it' means a valid (כשר) פסח, not a disqualified (פסול) one.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the verse says: 'And you shall not break a bone in it.' 'In it' means a valid one, not a disqualified one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The extra word בו narrows the prohibition to a valid פסח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פסח that became impure is פסול. The word בו teaches that the prohibition of breaking a bone applies only to a כשר פסח, so breaking a bone of an impure one is not a prohibition and carries no lashes.

keyTerms.meaning: And you shall not break a bone in it (שמות יב:מו)

steps.whatToRemember: No lashes for breaking a bone of an impure פסח, because the word בו limits the prohibition to a כשר פסח.

phrases.english: As the verse says:
"And you shall not break a bone in it";
"in it": in a valid one, and not in a disqualified one.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר קְרָא וְעֶצֶם לֹא תִשְׁבְּרוּ בוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word בו limits the bone-breaking prohibition to a כשר פסח and excludes a פסול (impure) one.

steps.title: A ברייתא records the 'in it' derivation
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the same derivation, 'in it' means a valid פסח and not a disqualified one, as the first opinion before רבי disagrees.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'And you shall not break a bone in it.' 'In it' means a valid one, not a disqualified one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that contains the derivation just given. It is setting up a second, competing derivation from רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This repetition does a new job. It presents the בו derivation as one side of a תנאים dispute, so the גמרא can compare it with רבי's approach in the next step.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"And you shall not break a bone in it";
"in it": in a valid one, and not in a disqualified one.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן וְעֶצֶם לֹא תִשְׁבְּרוּ בוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Cites a ברייתא matching step 18, which opens a dispute with רבי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תנא קמא: the word בו limits the prohibition to a כשר פסח.

steps.title: רבי: the prohibition applies to whatever is fit for eating
steps.stepSummary: רבי learns the rule from the nearby verse about eating. Whatever is fit to be eaten has the bone-breaking prohibition, and what is not fit to be eaten does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי says: 'In one house it shall be eaten ... and you shall not break a bone in it.' Whatever is fit for eating has the prohibition of breaking a bone, and whatever is not fit for eating does not.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי gives a different derivation for the same basic idea. He ties bone-breaking to the eating mentioned in the same verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא's test is 'is the פסח valid?' רבי's test is 'is it fit to be eaten?' Since the verse speaks of eating and then of breaking a bone, the prohibition follows the eating.

keyTerms.meaning: In one house it shall be eaten

steps.confusionAlert: רבי and the תנא קמא agree that an ordinary impure פסח has no bone-breaking prohibition. They differ only in which test they use, and that difference matters only in special cases.

phrases.english: Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi] says:
"In one house it shall be eaten ...
and you shall not break a bone in it."
Whatever is fit for eating
is subject to [the prohibition of] breaking a bone,
and whatever is not fit for eating
is not subject to [the prohibition of] breaking a bone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a competing derivation to the תנא קמא's בו reading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The bone-breaking prohibition depends on whether the פסח is ראוי לאכילה.

steps.title: What is the practical difference between the two derivations?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks in what case the 'valid' test and the 'fit for eating' test would give different results.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The two opinions seem to reach the same result, so the גמרא asks where they would actually differ in practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a valid פסח is eaten and a disqualified one is not, so both tests match. The גמרא wants a case where the two tests split.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the practical difference between them?

phrases.english: What is [the difference] between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical difference between steps 19 and 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where 'כשר' and 'ראוי לאכילה' give different rulings

steps.title: רבי ירמיה: the difference is a פסח brought in impurity
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה says the two views differ about a פסח offered when most of the people are impure. The גמרא begins to explain how the 'valid' view handles it, and this passage breaks off mid-sentence.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: A פסח brought in impurity is the difference between them. According to the one who says 'valid' ...
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה names the case where the two tests split. The last words begin the explanation, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פסח הבא בטומאה is an unusual פסח. It is offered and eaten even though the people are impure, so it does not fit neatly into either category. Each test (valid, or fit for eating) may sort it differently, and the גמרא is about to spell out each side.

keyTerms.meaning: A פסח offered when most of the nation is impure
There is a difference between them
According to the one who says

steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse a פסח הבא בטומאה with an ordinary פסח that became impure. The first is offered on purpose in a state of טומאה because most of the people are impure. The second is simply disqualified.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
A Pesach that is brought in impurity
is [the difference] between them.
According to the one who says [the prohibition depends on its being] valid ...
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה פֶּסַח הַבָּא בְּטוּמְאָה אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 21 and begins explaining each view's ruling.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The practical difference is a פסח הבא בטומאה. The detailed explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that 'valid' and 'fit for eating' are two separate tests that can split in unusual cases.
